questions.q: At 11 pm you discover a bug in a new feature. It was behind a flag. What is the fastest, safest move?
questions.hint: Does the code have to change, or only a switch?

options.text: Turn the flag off
options.why: The code doesn't change, so there is no new risk, and it takes seconds.

options.text: Do a rollback deploy to the previous version
options.why: It would work, but it is slow and the rollback is risky too. Avoiding that is the whole point of a flag.

options.text: Wait until morning and write a hotfix
options.why: Customers would suffer all night.

options.text: Restart the server
options.why: A restart brings back the same buggy code.

questions.q: Which of these correctly describes a kill switch?
questions.hint: Who changes it in an emergency, and how?

options.text: It can be changed without a deploy, and the app takes a fallback path when it is off
options.why: These are the two core requirements for an emergency off-switch.

options.text: It lives in a config file, and changing it needs a full deploy
options.why: In an emergency you can't wait for a deploy.

options.text: A flag you delete once the feature reaches 100%
options.why: That is a release flag. A kill switch is permanent, because you will need it again.

options.text: A button hidden only in Vue
options.why: If the API stays open on the server, nothing has actually been switched off.

questions.q: In the code below, users sometimes get the new checkout and sometimes the old one. Why?
questions.hint: What number will the same user get the second time around?

options.text: A new random number on every request, so the same user's result changes
options.why: Hashing the user id and flag name would give a stable result.

options.text: random_int() is slow
options.why: Speed isn't the problem here. The stability of the result is.

options.text: The value of $percent is wrong
options.why: Even with the right percentage, a random number differs every time.

options.text: The flag name isn't in English
options.why: The language of the name doesn't matter.

questions.q: Which of these are part of the right way to roll out a new checkout slowly?
questions.hint: Who goes first, and then what percentage?

options.text: Team only first, then 1%, 25%, and finally 100%
options.why: If you check error rate and orders at each step, the damage stays small.

options.text: Check the metrics at every step and turn the flag off if they get worse
options.why: That is the main purpose of a slow rollout: catching problems while the damage is limited.

options.text: Remove the flag and the old code once you reach 100%
options.why: If you don't, flag debt builds up.

options.text: Open it to all users at once and only use the flag if there is a problem
options.why: The damage then reaches everyone, and you lose the benefit of a slow rollout.

questions.q: A flagged checkout button is hidden in Vue. The API route has no flag check. What can a curious user do?
questions.hint: Who controls the browser: you or the user?

options.text: Send the request by hand and use the closed feature
options.why: Anything in the browser is in the user's hands. Only a check on the server can refuse the request.

options.text: Nothing, because the button is hidden
options.why: Hiding a button removes a shortcut, not the URL behind it.

options.text: Nothing, because Vue sends the flag with every request
options.why: A request typed by hand carries whatever its author writes; the server cannot trust the client.

options.text: Only users in the percentage bucket can do it
options.why: The bucket is only checked if the server asks. This route never asks.

questions.q: A release flag reached 100% two months ago and is still in the code. What should you do now?
questions.hint: The flag's job is over. Does it still belong in the code?

options.text: Remove the flag and the old path, and keep only the new code
options.why: A finished flag is debt. Removing it simplifies the code and cuts tests.

options.text: Leave it. You never know when you'll need it
options.why: The old path often no longer works, and it is dangerous if switched on by mistake.

options.text: Add a few more flags to keep everything under control
options.why: It only adds combinations and tangles things further.

options.text: Set the flag to true and forget about it
options.why: The debt is still there. If someone sets it to false by mistake, the broken path runs.

questions.q: What is wrong with the code below?
questions.hint: Which database would this code connect to if you ran it on staging?

options.text: The address and password are written in the code: they go into git, and staging would hit the prod database too
options.why: If config lived outside the code, neither risk would exist.

options.text: You shouldn't use const; a static property would be fine
options.why: The problem isn't what kind of declaration it is. The value sits inside the code.

options.text: PDO is outdated; you should use Doctrine DBAL
options.why: The library doesn't matter. Writing the value in code is just as bad with DBAL.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, it is an internal host
options.why: Internal or not, the password stays in git history forever.

questions.q: Tests passed on staging, but the app broke after deploying to prod. The team made a separate build for each environment. What is the best fix?
questions.hint: Are the thing that was tested and the thing that ran the same?

options.text: Build one image, run it in every environment, and differ only through env variables
options.why: Exactly what was tested on staging is what ships to prod.

options.text: Also run the prod build on staging for testing
options.why: There are still two separate builds, and they will still differ.

options.text: Stop deploying when tests pass
options.why: Stopping deploys isn't a fix. It just avoids the problem.

options.text: Fix it by changing the code directly on prod
options.why: That increases drift and creates even more different code.

questions.q: Which of these values should go in the Symfony secrets vault (or a secret manager)?
questions.hint: Who is hurt if it leaks?

options.text: The payment gateway API key
options.why: If it leaks, someone else can make transactions in your name.

options.text: The database password
options.why: If it leaks, all your data is at risk.

options.text: The JWT signing private key
options.why: If it leaks, anyone can forge tokens.

options.text: PAYMENT_TIMEOUT=5
options.why: Leaking it does no harm, so it can stay in .env as a safe default.

questions.q: What could go wrong in this Symfony code?
questions.hint: What type is an env variable?

options.text: An env value is a string; without the int: processor the type doesn't match (or the conversion you expect doesn't happen)
options.why: You need #[Autowire(env: 'int:PAYMENT_TIMEOUT')].

options.text: Autowire doesn't work without readonly
options.why: Autowire has nothing to do with readonly.

options.text: #[Autowire(env: ...)] doesn't exist in Symfony
options.why: It does exist. It is the modern way to inject env variables.

options.text: Env variables can't be read in code, only in YAML
options.why: You can read them in code too, with #[Autowire(env: ...)].

questions.hint: Why are staging and prod running down different paths?

options.text: Using the same image on staging and prod, and keeping the same list of env variables
options.why: The same code and the same kind of config run in both places.

options.text: Using if (APP_ENV === 'prod') to keep a separate code path for prod
options.why: The prod path never runs on staging, so drift grows.

options.text: Logging into the server to edit .env.local by hand when needed
options.why: Nobody notices that change, and six months later nobody knows why that server is different.

options.text: Using the cheapest database version on staging
options.why: With different versions, queries and behavior can differ too.

questions.q: Which rules are good candidates for moving into data?
questions.hint: They change often, are simple, and a mistake costs little.

options.text: The amount above which delivery is free
options.why: A single number that changes often, and a mistake costs little.

options.text: The discount percentage per product category (with the ceiling in code)
options.why: It changes often and business staff can change it. With the cap in code, it is safe.

options.text: The VAT calculation
options.why: It carries legal risk and a mistake does direct damage. Keep it in code, with review and tests.

options.text: The order in which money is deducted from balances
options.why: That is a procedure, not a chart. It involves state and ordering, so it stays in code.

questions.q: What danger is there in the code below?
questions.hint: What would the code do if someone wrote 100 in the data?

options.text: There is no ceiling on the discount, so a wrong number in the data is applied directly
options.why: A cap in code like min($percent, 30) would have stopped the damage from a typo.

options.text: You should use while instead of foreach
options.why: The kind of loop isn't the problem.

options.text: evaluate() never returns a bool
options.why: A condition gives a bool-like result, and that is fine.

options.text: Rules can't be stored in a database
options.why: They can. The problem is the lack of safeguards, not that the rules sit in the database.

questions.q: The marketing team wants to change a rule. Which order is safe?
questions.hint: Where is the chance to test against past events?

options.text: Write a new version, test, dry-run on the last 30 days, get approval, go live on a date
options.why: Each step catches a different kind of mistake, and the old version makes a rollback possible.

options.text: Overwrite the existing row with the new value
options.why: You lose the previous version, so auditing and rollback both become impossible.

options.text: Change it on the admin page and have it live in production immediately
options.why: Without tests or approval, a typo does direct damage.

options.text: Change it on staging only and see what happens
options.why: Staging doesn't have production's data. A dry run uses real old orders.

questions.q: The rule language slowly gains variables, loops and functions. What is this problem called, and what is the risk?
questions.hint: Does a "program" stored in a database have a debugger?

options.text: The inner-platform effect: a weak, untested programming language grows inside your data
options.why: Left in code, a complex rule would get tests, a debugger and review.

options.text: Cache stampede
options.why: That is a cache problem, not a rule-language problem.

options.text: Config drift
options.why: That is environments drifting apart from each other.

options.text: No problem, the rules are just getting more powerful
options.why: More power means more responsibility, and without tests that is a risk.

questions.q: Which precautions are right when you run rules with ExpressionLanguage?
questions.hint: A condition string is really a small piece of code.

options.text: Let only trusted staff change rules
options.why: A condition is code; whoever can write it can change the behavior.

options.text: Check with lint() before saving
options.why: Bad syntax is caught on the admin page, not in production.

options.text: Pass a small facts DTO, not the entity
options.why: The rule sees only what it needs, and rules in the database don't break when the entity changes.

options.text: Evaluate text typed by a customer as an expression
options.why: Running user input as an expression is dangerous.
